identity.title: Passive leg raise: hemodynamic response (BP/pulse pressure or POCUS VTI rise >=10-12%) within 60-90 s of raising legs 45 deg from semi-recumbent

technique.how: Start semi-recumbent (trunk 45 deg) and record a baseline flow measure (LVOT VTI by POCUS or monitor CO; pulse pressure is a weaker surrogate). Using the bed controls, lower the trunk flat and raise both legs to 45 deg without touching the patient; re-measure within 30-90 s at peak effect, then return to baseline and confirm values fall back. Positive: CO/VTI rise >=10%.
technique.prerequisites: A real-time flow measurement (VTI, CO monitor) is needed for accuracy; adjustable bed; patient tolerates supine positioning; no pain or agitation during the maneuver.
technique.contraindications: Raised intracranial pressure, intra-abdominal hypertension, lower-limb trauma/amputation or venous compression stockings (blunt venous return), and inability to lie flat.

interpretation.positive_finding: A PLR-induced rise in CO/VTI >=10% predicts that a fluid bolus will raise cardiac output (pooled sensitivity ~85%, specificity ~91%) and supports a preload-dependent state such as hypovolemia or early sepsis. It says nothing about whether fluids are needed or safe, only that they would raise output.
interpretation.negative_finding: No CO rise argues against fluid responsiveness and against giving further fluid; consider cardiogenic causes, vasoplegia, or already-adequate preload.
interpretation.pitfalls: Assessing with pulse pressure/BP alone has sensitivity of only ~56-58%, so a negative BP-based PLR does not exclude fluid responsiveness; peak effect is brief (about 1 min), so continuous or immediate measurement is required; intra-abdominal hypertension, wrong starting position, and pain (sympathetic stimulation) give false results.
interpretation.changes_what: Positive PLR with hypotension/AKI supports a fluid trial; negative PLR should stop empiric boluses and shift attention to cardiac dysfunction, vasoplegia, or obstruction.

estimates.target_condition: Fluid responsiveness (CO rise after volume expansion); PLR assessed by change in cardiac output, threshold ~>=10%
estimates.population: 21 studies, 991 adults with acute circulatory failure (mostly ICU, ventilated and spontaneously breathing), 995 fluid challenges; CO by echo, pulse contour, bioreactance, Doppler or thermodilution
estimates.reference_standard: Increase in cardiac output after a fluid challenge (study-defined, typically >=15%)
estimates.computed_from: LR+ = 0.85/(1-0.91) = 9.4; LR- = (1-0.85)/0.91 = 0.16; from pooled sensitivity 0.85 and specificity 0.91 (AUROC 0.95; best threshold CO rise >=10 +/- 2%)
estimates.quote: For the PLR-induced changes in CO, the pooled sensitivity was 0.85 (0.81-0.88) and the pooled specificity was 0.91 (0.88-0.93)

estimates.target_condition: Fluid responsiveness; PLR assessed by change in arterial pulse pressure
estimates.population: 8 studies, 432 fluid challenges in adults with acute circulatory failure (ICU)
estimates.reference_standard: Increase in cardiac output after a fluid challenge (study-defined)
estimates.computed_from: LR+ = 0.56/(1-0.83) = 3.3; LR- = (1-0.56)/0.83 = 0.53; from pooled sensitivity 0.56 and specificity 0.83 (AUROC 0.77). Sensitivity CI printed as 0.49-0.53 in abstract (typographical; does not bracket point estimate) so left null
estimates.quote: For the PLR-induced changes in PP (8 studies, 432 fluid challenges), the pooled sensitivity was 0.56 (0.49-0.53), the pooled specificity was 0.83 (0.77-0.88)

estimates.target_condition: Fluid responsiveness; PLR assessed by any technique (overall pooled)
estimates.population: 23 studies, 1013 adults, 1034 fluid challenges; ICU/OR patients, ventilated and spontaneously breathing
estimates.reference_standard: Fluid challenge as gold standard for responders vs non-responders
estimates.quote: pooled sensitivity of 86% (95% CI, 79-92), pooled specificity of 92% (95% CI, 88-96)

estimates.target_condition: Fluid responsiveness; PLR assessed by change in pulse pressure (subgroup)
estimates.population: Subgroup of the 23-study meta-analysis using pulse pressure change as the PLR readout
estimates.reference_standard: Fluid challenge as gold standard for responders vs non-responders
estimates.quote: sensitivity of 58% [95% CI, 44-70] and specificity of 83% [95% CI, 68-92]

sources.citation: Monnet X, Marik P, Teboul JL. Passive leg raising for predicting fluid responsiveness: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Intensive Care Med. 2016;42(12):1935-1947.
Cherpanath TG, Hirsch A, Geerts BF, et al. Predicting Fluid Responsiveness by Passive Leg Raising: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of 23 Clinical Trials. Crit Care Med. 2016;44(5):981-991.

safety_scope.do_not_use_when: Raised intracranial pressure, intra-abdominal hypertension, unstable pelvic/leg fractures, or when no flow measurement is available and a BP-only result would drive fluid decisions.
safety_scope.escalation_warning: A fluid-responsive patient can still have cardiogenic or obstructive shock; hypotension that does not respond to a fluid trial, or a negative PLR with hypoperfusion, needs vasoactive support and definitive diagnostics now.
safety_scope.interobserver_note: Accuracy depends on the readout: continuous flow measurement (VTI/CO) is reproducible; BP/PP-based and clinical eyeballing are not; VTI measurement itself has operator-dependent variability of roughly 10%, near the decision threshold.

extraction_notes: Sens/spec entered as percent (quotes preserve the decimal fractions used by Monnet 2016). Two overlapping meta-analyses are included because they use different pooling methods and study sets and agree closely; CO-based and PP-based readouts are kept as separate rows because performance differs materially. Monnet 2016 gives a sensitivity CI for PP of 0.49-0.53 in the abstract, which is internally inconsistent (does not include 0.56), so that CI is left null. No estimate is entered for the bedside BP-cuff (systolic BP) readout specifically; both reviews indicate PP-based assessment is inferior. Pubmed lists Monnet 2016 with year 2017 in some fields; the print citation is Intensive Care Med 2016;42:1935. The POCUS-VTI variant is a pocus-type technique but this record is typed 'functional'; operator skill assumptions are stated in interobserver_note.
